docs.title: regshot-rs
docs.text:
Fast, N-snapshot Windows registry comparison. A modern Rust reimplementation of Regshot: registry only (no filesystem scanning), built around an N-way diff engine instead of the classic two-shot comparison, with a complete CLI, an interactive TUI, a self-contained HTML report, template-driven output, and an MCP server for agents.

View on GitHub Getting started

Early scaffolding

This project is under active development. The core data model, interning, and N-way diff engine (regshot-core) are implemented and tested. The capture backend, report templates, TUI, GUI, and MCP server are being built out — see the changelog for exactly what works today, and the architecture page for how the pieces fit together.

docs.title: Why another Regshot
docs.text:
Upstream Regshot compares exactly two snapshots at a time, using an O(n·m) nested-loop comparison over a mutable linked tree — a structural limit that has nothing to do with performance and everything to do with the data model: a match flag mutated in place during comparison simply cannot represent a third snapshot. regshot-rs starts from a different model: snapshots are immutable, flat, sorted arrays, and comparing any number of them is a single linear merge-join.

  • N snapshots, not two

    Compare a whole sequence — before, during, after, after-reboot — in one timeline, not a chain of two-shot diffs.

  • A real diff engine

    A merge-join over sorted, interned paths: linear in the number of entries, not quadratic.

  • CLI, TUI, and MCP — one engine

    Everything the TUI or a report template can do is reachable as a CLI flag or an MCP tool. Nothing is TUI-only.

  • x86, x64, and ARM64

    All three are Rust Tier 1 targets, built and tested natively in CI — including on windows-11-arm.

docs.title: The registry-only decision
docs.text: Upstream Regshot optionally scans a list of filesystem directories alongside the registry. regshot-rs deliberately does not: registry diffing and filesystem diffing are different problems that happened to share a report format, and cutting one lets the other get simpler and more correct everywhere it touches — one entity model, five change categories instead of eleven, one capture trait instead of two. See No filesystem scanning for the full reasoning and what to use instead.

docs.title: WOW64 views: the bug this tool is built to avoid
docs.text: On 64-bit Windows the registry has two views, and a 32-bit process's reads of e.g. HKLM\Software are silently redirected to HKLM\Software\Wow6432Node — no error, no warning. A 32-bit build and a 64-bit build of a naive registry differ capture different registries at the same path, and diffing one against the other produces a completely fabricated changeset. This is load-bearing enough that it is encoded in the type system, not left to a runtime check — see Registry views.

docs.text: This page tracks what's actually implemented, not just planned — see the repository's CHANGELOG.md-equivalent (GitHub Releases) for the canonical, versioned record once tagged releases exist.

docs.title: Implemented and tested
docs.text:
• Core data model (regshot-core): interned, WOW64-view-rooted PathId/NameId, immutable sorted Snapshot/KeyEntry/ValueEntry, content-addressed BlobStore.
  • N-way diff engine: the TimelineMatrix merge-join, all five change categories, a brute-force reference oracle, and a proptest property suite covering reflexivity, the undo-restores-prior-state property, N-way/pairwise consistency, category disjointness, and WOW64-view non-aliasing.
  • The .rshot on-disk format: rkyv-archived, zstd-compressed, magic/version header, with a decompression-bomb guard.
  • Capture trait boundary (regshot-core::capture, regshot-capture): the RegistrySource/KeySink traits, a tested SyntheticSource used by every test on every platform, and — Windows only — the real Win32 backend (RegEnumKeyExW/RegEnumValueW, explicit KEY_WOW64_64KEY/KEY_WOW64_32KEY).
  • Legacy .hiv/.hivu import: reads upstream Regshot's ANSI and Unicode snapshot formats, reverse-engineered from upstream's own source (see regshot-core::legacy's module doc), including the ANSI→UTF-16LE value-data conversion needed to preserve this project's storage invariant and cycle-safe iterative tree walking upstream's own loader never bothered with.
  • Output emitters (regshot-report): txt/json/html report templates via minijinja (html embeds the report as JSON and renders it with hand-written vanilla JS — virtualized timeline/pairwise table, search, category/kind/view facets, a detail panel with prefix/suffix diff highlighting, dual light/dark theme using the exact palette in docs/guide/reading-the-report.md), hand-written reg4/reg5/ps1 undo-redo script renderers (with the mixed-WOW64-view refusal for .reg, and a header comment naming the view and the reg.exe /reg:32//reg:64 invocation needed to import it correctly — reg4 is REGEDIT4/ANSI, upstream Regshot's own format; non-Latin-1 REG_SZ text falls back to hex(1): with the raw UTF-16LE bytes rather than losing data, lossless on any NT-based Windows), and the regshot query/MCP query_changes filter expression language (category/path/name/view/kind/data/snapshot fields; ==, !=, starts_with, contains, in (…), &&/||). ReportChange now also carries rendered before/after value text (from_data/to_data), which json and html show; txt deliberately doesn't, to stay byte-comparable with upstream 1.9.1's plain-text output.
  • Installer-script templates (regshot-report::installer): nsis and inno render one script holding both an installer (replays the diff by default; --direction undo swaps) and an uninstaller (its exact reverse). Both handle mixed-WOW64-view changesets natively: NSIS through SetRegView, Inno through HKLM64/HKLM32 roots. Inno's uninstaller restores values through RegSetValueExW from generated [Code], because [Registry]'s uninsdelete* flags can't restore modified or deleted values and RegWriteBinaryValue corrupts bytes ≥ 0x80 via the ANSI codepage. Anything a format can't express exactly is refused with a list of the offending entries, never dropped. unl writes Regshot-Advanced's removal-list format. All three are also available through the MCP export tool. Windows CI compiles the nsis/inno output with the real toolchains and round-trips it against a live registry in both views — see docs/guide/undo-and-installers.md.
  • CI on every architecture and the MSRV: the Windows job now builds and tests on x64, 32-bit x86 (running under WOW64) and native ARM64 runners. A new MSRV job checks that the workspace builds on its minimum Rust version and regshot-gui on 1.95. It found the declared minimum of 1.85 was wrong (dependencies need 1.88), so the workspace now declares 1.88. The new x86 leg also found that the 32-bit build had never compiled: the .rshot decompression cap was 4 GiB as a usize. It's now 1 GiB on 32-bit targets, so the i686 release artifact builds.
  • Fuzzing: cargo-fuzz targets for .rshot reading, .hiv/.hivu import, the filter language and regshot.ini migration. The two file-format targets also check a write-and-read round trip, and they start from generated valid seeds. CI fuzzes each target for 30 s on every PR and for 10 min daily with a persisted corpus. See docs/development/contributing.md.
  • GUI reads the settings file: the settings model moves out of the CLI into a new regshot-config crate shared by both interfaces. The GUI now starts from [capture] (hives, views, skip and whitelist) and [report] generalize_paths, and says so in the status bar when it falls back to a default.
  • Start menu: regshot tui with no snapshots shows a menu instead of an error. It can open snapshots here in the explorer, take a snapshot (Windows), compare to an HTML report, export a script or installer, import a .hiv, show a snapshot's details, reopen a triaged set, or open the GUI or the settings file. Nothing loads until you choose, each item shows its equivalent command, and every action runs through the same code as that command. With no terminal attached it prints the help and exits 2. A bare regshot always prints the help and exits 2: a subcommand is required, so a script can never land in an interactive session by accident.
  • TUI timeline view and fuzzy search: s toggles the change table between pairwise and a timeline of every change across all snapshots, with one state glyph per snapshot. / is now a ranked fuzzy search (nucleo), and n/N step through matches best first. The table gains a view column, so a 64-bit entry and its 32-bit namesake no longer look like one row listed twice. The TUI guide is rewritten from the real behavior; it still described the TUI as unimplemented.
  • TUI triage persistence: marks are saved as you make them to a .regshot-triage-<hash>.json sidecar next to the snapshots, keyed by their contents and order. V jumps to the next untriaged change, X, X clears all marks (it used to be a single V), and the facets pane shows the triaged count. regshot query --triaged only|exclude filters by the same marks.
  • Shell completions and man pages: regshot completion <bash|zsh|fish|powershell|elvish> prints a completion script and regshot man --out-dir <dir> writes regshot.1 plus a page per subcommand, both generated from the clap definition itself. Release archives now include both, under completions/ and man/. See docs/getting-started/installation.md.
  • ndjson-ecs output (regshot diff --template ndjson-ecs, MCP generate_report): one ECS 9.5 registry event per change. Values carry typed registry.data: decoded strings, decimal numbers, or base64 bytes. Custom regshot.* fields hold the category, view, interesting rule, snapshot pair and previous value. See docs/reference/formats.md.
  • Known-interesting heuristics fixes: per-user rules now match under every HKU\<SID>\ user hive, not just HKCU. Captures default to HKLM + HKU, so a per-user Run entry was going unflagged. A prefix rule also no longer matches a sibling that merely shares its prefix: …\RunOnce was being labeled Run.
  • The GUI (regshot-gui, egui/eframe): a desktop shell with a snapshot list (open .rshot, import .hiv/.hivu, reorder, details), capture on Windows with live progress, Compare (renders the HTML report and opens it), and Export (every script template). It goes through the same library paths as the CLI, uses the shared palette (regshot-report::palette, which a test keeps in step with the report's CSS), and is covered by headless egui_kittest UI tests. See docs/guide/gui.md.
  • Shared script rendering (regshot-report::script): the CLI export, the MCP export tool and the GUI render and encode scripts through one render_script. ps1 scripts are now written with a UTF-8 BOM. Before this they were BOM-less, and Windows PowerShell 5.1 reads such scripts in the system ANSI code page, corrupting any non-ASCII key name or value an undo script restores.
  • View-mismatch check everywhere: query, export and tui now refuse snapshots captured with different WOW64 view sets, as diff always did, and gain the same --allow-view-mismatch override. So do the MCP diff, suggest_interesting, query_changes, generate_report and export tools, which previously skipped the check entirely (allow_view_mismatch: true to override). An export across mismatched sets would have produced an undo script that deletes every entry in the view only one side captured. The check lives in regshot_core::check_view_sets.
  • REG_EXPAND_SZ expanded form: capture records the value of each environment variable the snapshot's REG_EXPAND_SZ values reference. It never records the whole environment, which often holds credentials. This is stored in .rshot format v2, and version-1 files still load. The report (json from_expanded/to_expanded, and the HTML detail panel), the TUI and MCP get_value_data show each value expanded with ExpandEnvironmentStrings semantics, and list any variable that wasn't set at capture. regshot info lists what was recorded.
  • HTML report deep links, hex dump, and (NULL!): the URL hash mirrors the whole view (mode, search, facets, selected row), with a Copy link button, and opening or pasting a link restores that view. The selection now stays on the same row across filter changes. Byte-list values get a hex dump with differing bytes marked, and each side shows its size. A present-but-zero-length value shows upstream's (NULL!), using the new from_size/to_size byte counts on ReportChange, which the json output carries too. The timeline also no longer merges a 64-bit value with its 32-bit namesake into a single row. Headless-browser tests cover all of it.
  • Known-interesting-location heuristics (regshot-report::interesting): a curated table (Run/RunOnce, services, scheduled tasks, AppInit_DLLs, Image File Execution Options, Winlogon, LSA packages, shell extensions) matched on (hive, path) — deliberately not on WOW64 view, since a redirected path reads identically through both views and a view-restricted rule would miss every 32-bit installer's entry. Surfaced via ReportChange's new interesting field, a ⚠ badge/facet/detail-panel entry in the HTML report, regshot diff --only-interesting (narrows the report and recomputes its summary counts), and the MCP suggest_interesting tool (findings grouped by rule, ranked by count).
  • Path generalization (regshot-report::generalize): regshot diff --generalize rewrites C:\Users\<name>\AppData\{Roaming,Local}\… to %AppData%/%LocalAppData% (any drive letter) and collapses a per-user SID under HKU\S-1-5-21-… to HKU\<user>, applied to the report's path/from_data/to_data only — never the underlying .rshot data. Defaults to [report] generalize_paths (itself true by default); --no-generalize overrides it in either direction, unlike --allow-capture's OR-only merge, since this flag pair is properly negatable.
  • REG_EXPAND_SZ readable text (report_value_text): the report (txt/json/html) and query's data field now decode REG_EXPAND_SZ the same way as REG_SZ, instead of the hex(2):… byte list every other non-REG_SZ/REG_DWORD type falls back to. reg4/reg5 export is deliberately unchanged (reg_value_literal, still hex(2):…) — that's what real regedit.exe itself writes for REG_EXPAND_SZ, since .reg's quoted-string syntax has no way to mark a value as expandable. --generalize picks this up automatically, since it operates on whatever quoted text the report renders.
  • The TUI (regshot-tui): a ratatui interactive explorer — windowed table over the timeline (never renders more than the visible viewport regardless of dataset size), snapshot rail, facets pane, detail pane, vim-native keybindings, tested via insta frame snapshots against synthetic data.
  • regshot config: TOML config file (--init), and a migration reader for upstream's regshot.ini (--migrate) that handles both upstream's and Regshot-Advanced's incompatible [SkipRegKey] dialects, with filesystem-related keys surfaced as warnings rather than silently dropped. Read back in as per-command defaults by shot/diff/mcp, CLI flags still taking precedence — see docs/reference/configuration.md for the exact merge per field.
  • MCP server (regshot-mcp), both transports: load_snapshot, take_snapshot (live capture, Windows-only, gated behind --allow-capture, sharing its orchestration — regshot-capture::capture_snapshot — with regshot shot so the two entry points can't drift apart on what "capture" means), list_snapshots, diff (per-transition category counts, never row-level detail), query_changes (the filter language above), suggest_interesting (the known-interesting heuristics above, grouped findings), get_value_data, describe_filter_syntax, generate_report (txt/json/html), and export (reg4/reg5/ps1/unl/nsis/inno) — 27 tests exercising every tool through the real JSON-RPC protocol. The streamable HTTP transport (--http host:port) is loopback-only unless --allow-non-loopback, requires a locally-generated, persisted bearer token unless --no-auth (itself refused on a non-loopback bind), and relies on rmcp's own Host-header allowlist as the DNS-rebinding mitigation — see docs/guide/mcp-server.md's security model. Run by hand in a terminal, the stdio server says what it is and prints the claude mcp add/codex mcp add lines to register it, instead of looking hung; Ctrl-D before any client connects exits cleanly. --http prints a ready-to-paste connect command. The server identifies itself as regshot-rs in the MCP handshake (it previously reported the SDK's own name, rmcp). The README has config examples for Claude Code, Codex, opencode, Cursor, VS Code and Gemini CLI, and the guide shows how to keep the HTTP server running as a Task Scheduler task or a systemd user unit.
  • CLI surface (regshot-cli): the full command shape from the reference parses today, and every subcommand is wired to a real backend except shot, which needs the live Windows registry and only runs on that platform.

  • Full workspace lint posture (unsafe_code denied outside the Win32 FFI boundary, unwrap/expect/panic/indexing denied in library code), CI covering fmt/clippy/test/doc on Linux and a build+test smoke check on Windows x64.

  • Localization groundwork (regshot-i18n): every human-facing string in the GUI, start menu, explorer, command-line messages, and the txt/html reports is a Fluent message in locales/en.ftl. Machine output (JSON, NDJSON, CSV, scripts) is not translated. The language comes from --lang/REGSHOT_LANG, the settings file's new [ui] language, or the system, and falls back to English.

  • Plurals follow each language's CLDR rules, including those the HTML report's script counts in the browser.
  • Terminal columns are padded by display width, so double-width CJK labels line up.
  • The HTML report sets lang/dir and uses logical CSS properties, so right-to-left languages lay out mirrored.
  • Tests check that every message ID in the sources exists, that every message is used, and that translations use the same placeables as English.
  • regshot info now shows the capture time as a date instead of raw milliseconds (--json keeps the milliseconds).
  • 36 languages: every one of the 29 in upstream Regshot's language.ini, plus Korean, Arabic, Vietnamese, Indonesian, Romanian, Finnish and European Portuguese. Strings that mean the same in both programs come from upstream's human translators, credited in each file, and a test checks them against a vendored language.ini, decoding each section with the codepage it was written in (GBK, Big5, Shift-JIS, windows-125x). Where upstream was damaged or wrong (characters lost to cp1251, keyboard "keys" for registry keys), the fix and its reason are recorded. The rest is machine-translated and marked as such. A completeness test keeps every shipped language at every message.
  • regshot config --migrate carries upstream's [Setup] Language= into [ui] language.
  • System tags map to the shipped variant: zh-HK→zh-TW, nn→nb, sr→sr-Latn, pt→pt-BR.

  • See docs/development/translating.md for the language list.

  • GUI redesign: the window draws itself the same on Windows and Linux instead of following each platform's defaults.

  • Bundled fonts: Inter for text, JetBrains Mono for paths and values, and Phosphor icons.
  • Design tokens from the report's palette, a 4-point spacing grid and a small type scale.
  • Cards with radii matched to their controls, and a toolbar, sidebar and status bar.
  • Snapshot rows show the label, capture time, views and counts at a glance.
  • Screenshots in the GUI guide are rendered by an ignored test (cargo test -p regshot-gui --test screenshots -- --ignored).
  • Every language in the GUI:
  • Chinese, Japanese and Korean use bundled Noto Sans SC/TC/JP/KR, cut down to the characters the translations use. The interface language's own regional font comes first, so a character shared by several gets that language's form. A test fails when a translation gains a character its font lacks, and crates/regshot-gui/assets/fonts/subset.sh rebuilds the fonts.
  • Hebrew and Arabic read right to left. egui shapes Arabic letters but has no bidirectional layout, so the GUI runs the Unicode bidi algorithm itself: runs come out in visual order, numbers and Latin text keep their own direction, and brackets mirror. The whole window mirrors too: the sidebar moves to the right, and labels, rows and buttons start from the right. Long text is cut at its logical end.

  • Known gap: right-to-left text typed into a text field shows its words in typing order.

  • Faster capture. Everything a capture does besides calling the registry is about 5× faster: walking, interning and building a 106k-key, 161k-value tree went from 415 ms to 77 ms (cargo bench -p regshot-capture).

  • The walk passes each key's interned path down to its values and subkeys instead of building and re-parsing full path strings.
  • Names live in one arena, looked up by the hash of their folded form, and are folded without allocating when they're ASCII. Value data is deduplicated into one buffer.
  • One set of buffers serves the whole walk, so a key or value costs no allocation of its own.
  • The walk is written once against a small RawRegistry trait. The Win32 backend and the in-memory test registry both implement it, so tests and benchmarks run the real walk on any platform.
  • Skip and whitelist patterns fixed and faster. Patterns are compiled once and matched without building paths, and a skipped key's subtree is no longer read at all.
  • Fixed: a path with a hive, like the documented --whitelist-key 'HKLM\SOFTWARE\MyApp', never matched, so that example captured nothing. Paths now match with a short or long hive name, or without one to match under any hive.

  • Changed: a pattern no longer matches as a substring (Temp used to skip Attempt). As in upstream Regshot, it names whole keys: a path, or a key name anywhere.

  • Native capture where it's exact. Capture reads the registry through ntdll (NtOpenKeyEx, NtEnumerateKey, NtEnumerateValueKey, NtQueryKey) wherever that reads a view exactly as the Reg* API does, and through the Reg* API elsewhere.

  • The native calls see the physical tree. In a 64-bit process that's the 64-bit view, because the Reg* layer, not the kernel, redirects 32-bit-view opens. Under WOW64 both views work.
  • Windows CI compares the two backends key for key, in every view, on x64, x86 and ARM64, and logs whole-hive timings for each.
  • One CurrentControlSet. A snapshot holds the current control set once, as CurrentControlSet, instead of twice (the link and the ControlSetNNN it points to). That's the name that's correct when a script is replayed on another machine. .hiv imports, which hold it twice, are reduced the same way.
  • The control set's number is recorded in .rshot format v3 (v1 and v2 still load), shown by regshot info, the GUI and the start menu.

  • regshot diff notes when compared snapshots recorded different control sets.

  • Parallel capture. Each hive is walked on every core: keys near the root, and the subkeys of wide keys, are read by rayon workers into compact logs, which are then replayed into the snapshot in exactly the single-threaded walk's order. The snapshot is the same however many threads read it (a test compares them entry for entry), and RAYON_NUM_THREADS caps the count. On a 4-core Windows CI runner, HKLM's 64-bit view (648k keys, 1.09M values) now takes about 15 s instead of 49 s, and its 32-bit view 5 s instead of 33 s.

  • Smaller registry calls. Each call is offered only the buffer size its key needs, not the largest the walk has needed so far: the cost of a call grows with the length it's given. That alone made the native walk of HKLM 2.9× faster (17 s instead of 49 s on one thread).

  • Fixed: the native walker's "open links as themselves" mode followed them anyway: it needs OBJ_OPENLINK, not REG_OPTION_OPEN_LINK. Capture doesn't use the mode yet.

  • Incremental capture (opt-in). regshot shot --baseline before.rshot reuses the baseline's values for every key whose last write time hasn't changed, instead of reading them again. Every key is still visited, and the snapshot is the same one a full capture produces (a test compares them). It's opt-in, because a program can forge a key's last write time to hide a change. If the current control set changed since the baseline, nothing under CurrentControlSet is reused.

  • Each key's last write time is now captured and stored: .rshot format v4 (v1–v3 still load).

docs.title: Dropped
docs.text:
The differential test against the real Regshot.exe was dropped: it would need upstream's binary vendored and driven headlessly, for little gain over the existing format and diff tests.

If a guide or reference page describes a flag or behavior that isn't in the list above yet, it's documenting the intended, stable shape — most subcommands' argument parsing is already final even where their backend isn't built.

docs.title: FAQ
docs.text:
Why not just add N-snapshot support to upstream Regshot? : Upstream's comparison mutates a match flag on a linked tree during comparison — the reason it can compare exactly two snapshots is structural, not a missing feature flag. Fixing it means replacing the data model, at which point most of the C codebase around it needs to change too. See Architecture.

Where did filesystem scanning go? : Removed deliberately. See No filesystem scanning for the full reasoning and what to use instead.

Why does the 32-bit build matter if I'm on 64-bit Windows? : It doesn't, usually — prefer the x64 build, which captures both registry views by default. The 32-bit build exists for genuinely 32-bit Windows installs. See Registry views.

Can I still use my old .hiv/.hivu snapshots? : Yes — regshot import-hive reads both the ANSI and Unicode legacy formats and converts them to .rshot. See Formats.

Is the MCP server safe to run? : Default to stdio (no network surface at all). If you enable HTTP, read the security model first — it's written to be read before you flip that switch, not after something goes wrong.

Does this replace Procmon? : No, and it isn't trying to. Procmon does continuous, real-time, kernel-level monitoring via ETW. regshot-rs takes discrete snapshots and diffs them — a different tool for a different job. See No filesystem scanning.

Where can I track progress? : The changelog is kept honest about what's implemented versus planned.

docs.title: Migrating from Regshot
docs.text: This page is for users of either upstream Regshot 1.9.1 or the third-party Regshot-Advanced fork.

docs.title: Feature map
docs.text: Upstream / Advanced feature regshot-rs equivalent Two-shot compare N-way compare — pass any number of snapshots to regshot diff .hiv / .hivu .rshot — import old snapshots with regshot import-hive, see Formats regshot.ini TOML config — regshot config --migrate regshot.ini language.ini (~30 languages) Fluent-based i18n, importing existing translations (planned) Scan directories, SkipDir/SkipFile Removed. See No filesystem scanning Case-sensitive key comparison Fixed — registry comparison is case-insensitive, matching Windows' own semantics; see Architecture .tpl output templates (Advanced) minijinja-based templates, same concept, real template language — see Output templates WhitelistRegKey (Advanced) --whitelist-key, carried forward as-is — see Filtering noise GUI-only workflow CLI-complete: everything the GUI/TUI can do is a CLI flag — see Automation No agent/automation surface MCP server — see MCP server

docs.title: What's new, not just renamed
docs.text:
• WOW64-view-aware capture and comparison. Neither upstream nor Advanced model the 32-bit vs. 64-bit registry view distinction at all — see Registry views for why that's a real correctness gap, not a nice-to-have.
  • Timeline view. Only exists once you can compare more than two snapshots.
  • Path generalization and known-interesting-location heuristics — see Filtering noise.
  • x86, x64, and ARM64, all built and tested natively in CI.

docs.title: What's intentionally not carried forward
docs.text: Filesystem scanning — see No filesystem scanning for the full reasoning and alternatives. If your workflow depends on it, keep using upstream Regshot or Regshot-Advanced alongside a dedicated filesystem-diff tool.

docs.title: Known upstream bugs not reproduced
docs.text:
• Case-sensitive comparison of a case-insensitive registry (upstream carries a // TODO: case-insensitive compare? that was never resolved).
  • The registry-view aliasing bug this whole project exists partly to avoid — see Registry views.

These are deliberate divergences, not accidental ones; differences found in cross-testing that turn out to be upstream bugs get an explicit allow-list entry rather than being silently matched.

docs.title: No filesystem scanning
docs.text: If you're coming from upstream Regshot looking for --dirs, ScanDir1, or SkipDir: they don't exist here. This is the largest deliberate departure from upstream, and it's worth explaining rather than just declaring.

docs.title: What's cut
docs.text: Upstream Regshot optionally walks a ;-separated list of directories and emits six file/dir change categories (FILEADD, FILEDEL, FILEMODI, DIRADD, DIRDEL, DIRMODI) alongside the five registry ones. regshot-rs does not scan the filesystem at all: no scan-directory flags, no per-file/per-directory skip lists, no file hashing, no file/dir categories in the diff engine.

docs.title: Why
docs.text:
• It's a different problem wearing the same coat. Registry diffing is a bounded, API-enumerable, strongly-typed tree. Filesystem diffing is an unbounded walk over arbitrary mount points with its own permissions, reparse-point, and long-path failure modes. Sharing a report format made the two look like one feature. They never were.
  • It's where upstream's cost and its bugs concentrated. A long-standing bug where "C:" in the scan-dir list scanned the drive's current directory rather than its root, dir-chain mismatch warnings, and a checksum field that sat unused ("planned for the future") for over a decade were all filesystem code.
  • Purpose-built tools already do this well, and unlike registry snapshotting, they aren't scarce.
  • Everything downstream gets simpler: one entity kind instead of three, five change categories instead of eleven, one capture trait instead of two, one skip-list grammar, and a diff engine whose only identity key is (view, path, name).

docs.title: Legacy .hiv/.hivu files still carry a file chain
docs.text: Reading an old snapshot for migration means parsing past its file-chain section (the offsets are a linked chain, not a skippable block), so the importer walks it — and discards it, reporting how many entries were dropped rather than silently losing them. See Formats.

docs.title: What to use instead
docs.text:
Running one of these alongside regshot for the filesystem half is a perfectly good workflow — it's just not this tool's job:

  • robocopy /L or Get-ChildItem + Compare-Object for a quick before/after directory diff on Windows.
  • git diff over a directory you've committed to a throwaway repo, when you want a real content diff rather than just presence/attributes.
  • WinMerge for an interactive folder comparison.
  • Procmon for live, real-time filesystem (and registry) activity — see also the note on real-time monitoring being explicitly out of scope, below.

docs.title: Also out of scope, for the same reason
docs.text:
Real-time monitoring. Procmon and similar tools do continuous kernel-level capture via ETW or a minifilter driver — a fundamentally different tool with a different threat model, driver signing requirements, and event volume. regshot-rs's value is precisely that it isn't that: no driver, no agent, two (or more) points in time.

Hash whitelists and YARA scanning. Both operate on files, so both left with the filesystem.

docs.title: Workspace layout
docs.text:
regshot-rs/
├── crates/
│   ├── regshot-core/      # model, interning, diff engine — no OS deps, fully tested
│   ├── regshot-capture/   # Win32 registry scanner (cfg(windows)); synthetic source for tests
│   ├── regshot-report/    # template engine + HTML/text/reg/ps1/nsis/json emitters
│   ├── regshot-config/    # the settings file: model, location, loading, regshot.ini migration
│   ├── regshot-mcp/       # MCP server (stdio + streamable HTTP)
│   ├── regshot-tui/       # ratatui interactive explorer
│   ├── regshot-cli/       # the `regshot` binary — hosts the TUI too
│   └── regshot-gui/       # `regshot-gui` binary: egui shell (snapshots, capture, compare, export)
├── docs/                  # this site
└── .github/workflows/

regshot-core, regshot-report, and regshot-mcp's analysis half build on any platform. Only regshot-capture's Win32 backend is Windows-gated — so a Linux build can still load and compare .rshot files captured elsewhere, a capability upstream Regshot lacks entirely. This is also why development happens primarily on Linux: the core model, diff engine, template engine, and TUI are all testable without Windows at all.

docs.title: The core data model
docs.text:
Upstream Regshot's comparison mutates an in-place match flag on a linked tree during comparison — correct for two snapshots, structurally incapable of a third. regshot-rs starts from the opposite shape: immutable, flat, sorted arrays.

pub struct Snapshot {
    pub meta:   SnapMeta,
    pub keys:   Box<[KeyEntry]>,    // sorted by PathId
    pub values: Box<[ValueEntry]>,  // sorted by (PathId, NameId)
    pub blobs:  BlobStore,
}

Comparing snapshots is then a merge-join: linear in the total number of entries, and the same sweep whether you're comparing 2 snapshots or 20 — advance N cursors, emit one row per entity, derive its category from the transition. Every category (KeyAdd, KeyDel, ValAdd, ValDel, ValModi) is derived, never stored: Absent → Present is an add, Present → Absent is a delete, Present{h1} → Present{h2} with different hashes is a modification.

docs.title: Interning and WOW64 views
docs.text: Paths and value names are interned — case-folded for identity (fixing upstream's real case-sensitivity bug) while the interner keeps the first-seen spelling for display. Critically, every interned path is rooted under a RegView (registry-views.md), so HKLM\Software\Foo read through the 64-bit view and through the 32-bit view intern to two different, never-aliasing ids. The fabricated-changeset bug that motivated modeling views at all is prevented at the type level: there is no code path where a 32-bit-view entity can accidentally match a 64-bit-view one.

docs.title: The timeline
docs.text:
pub type State = Option<NonZeroU64>;   // presence + a content hash, or absence

pub struct TimelineMatrix {
    n_snapshots: usize,
    entities:    Box<[EntityId]>,
    states:      Box<[State]>,   // flattened row-major, stride n_snapshots
}

One allocation for the whole matrix rather than one small collection per row — at a million rows that difference is the whole ballgame. TimelineMatrix::changes(from, to) gives the pairwise view any two snapshots in the set; the same matrix serves the N-way timeline view without a second data path.

docs.title: Testing philosophy
docs.text: The diff engine gets two independent checks: a deliberately slow, obviously-correct O(n·m) nested-loop oracle, and proptest-generated snapshot pairs asserting the fast merge-join agrees with it on every input. Beyond agreement, a handful of properties are checked explicitly, including the one that matters most for a tool whose output undoes changes on a live system: undo(diff(s1, s2)) applied to s2 reconstructs s1 exactly. See the testing module and tests/ in regshot-core for the generator and the property suite.

docs.title: Platform capture boundary
docs.text:
pub trait RegistrySource {
    type Error: core::error::Error + From<IdSpaceExhausted>;
    fn walk<S: KeySink>(&self, hive: HiveRoot, view: RegView, sink: &mut S) -> Result<(), Self::Error>;
}

pub trait KeySink {
    type Key: Copy;
    fn root(&mut self, view: RegView, hive: HiveRoot) -> Result<Option<Self::Key>, IdSpaceExhausted>;
    fn key(&mut self, parent: Self::Key, name: &str) -> Result<Option<Self::Key>, IdSpaceExhausted>;
    fn value(&mut self, key: Self::Key, name: &str, kind: RegType, data: &[u8]) -> Result<(), IdSpaceExhausted>;
}

Generic over the sink (static dispatch), because the callback is invoked millions of times during a real scan: a dyn vtable hop per key/value is not free enough to pay for the whole registry. The sink hands back its own Key for each key, an interned path in the snapshot's case, and the walk passes it back for that key's values and subkeys. So the walk never builds a full path, and returning None for a key skips its whole subtree without reading it.

The walk itself is written once, in regshot-capture's walk module, against RawRegistry: the few calls a walk needs (open a key, query its buffer sizes, enumerate subkeys and values). On Windows, NtSource implements those calls over ntdll and Win32Source over the Reg* API. Capture uses NtSource wherever it reads a view exactly as the Reg* API does: every view except the 32-bit one in a 64-bit process, where only the Reg* layer redirects. tests/live_registry.rs checks that on every Windows architecture CI runs. SyntheticSource, an in-memory tree, implements them everywhere, so tests and benchmarks run the real walk on any platform. One set of buffers serves a whole walk, and names are decoded into a reused string, so a key or value costs no allocation of its own.

Capture walks each hive in parallel (walk_parallel): rayon workers read the keys near the root, and the subkeys of wide keys, into compact logs, and the calling thread replays the logs into the sink in the single-threaded walk's order. So the sink needs no locking, and a snapshot doesn't depend on the thread count.

Skip and whitelist patterns are compiled once into a small trie (regshot-capture's filter module). Each key's sink Key carries its position in that trie, so matching a key costs a comparison or two.

cargo bench -p regshot-capture measures everything except the registry calls: it walks a generated registry shaped like a real HKLM (about 106k keys and 161k values) and builds the snapshot.

docs.title: Rust workspace
docs.text:
cargo build --workspace
cargo test --workspace
cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets
cargo fmt --all -- --check

Requires the toolchain pinned in rust-toolchain.toml (currently 1.97.1, edition 2024, MSRV 1.88, except regshot-gui, which needs 1.95 for egui/eframe 0.36). cargo build/cargo test deny warnings by default via .cargo/config.toml's build.warnings = "deny"; cargo clippy is run without a blanket -D warnings so the workspace's deliberately-warn-level clippy::pedantic/clippy::cargo groups stay informational rather than build-breaking (see .github/workflows/ci.yml for the exact invocation and why).

docs.title: Docs site
docs.text:
The docs you're reading are built with mkdocs-material. Locally, with uv:

uv venv docs/.venv
source docs/.venv/bin/activate   # or docs\.venv\Scripts\activate on Windows
uv pip install -r docs/requirements.txt
mkdocs serve                     # live-reloading preview at http://127.0.0.1:8000
mkdocs build --strict            # what CI runs — fails on broken links

docs.title: Cross-platform notes
docs.text: Only regshot-capture's Windows backend needs a Windows host to build and test; everything else compiles and runs on Linux/macOS, which is how this project is developed day to day. CI builds and tests on Windows x64, on 32-bit x86 (running under WOW64 on an x64 runner), and on native ARM64 hardware (windows-11-arm). See Architecture for why the crate split makes that possible. A separate CI job checks that the declared minimum Rust versions still build: 1.88 for the workspace, and 1.95 for regshot-gui.

docs.title: License and provenance
docs.text:
The project is LGPL-2.1-or-later, matching upstream Regshot and Regshot-Advanced. If you're porting code or ideas from either:

  • Keep upstream copyright notices intact in any ported file, and add a provenance comment naming the source file and revision.
  • Every Rust source file starts with an SPDX header, // SPDX-License-Identifier: LGPL-2.1-or-later, as its first line. CI checks this.

docs.title: Code style
docs.text:
• cargo fmt and cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets clean, per Building — CI enforces both.
  • unsafe is denied workspace-wide except in regshot-capture, for the Win32 FFI boundary specifically. Every unsafe block there needs a // SAFETY: comment stating the invariant — clippy::undocumented_unsafe_blocks is deny in that one crate.
  • unwrap()/expect()/panic!()/direct indexing are denied in library code. Parsers that touch untrusted input (.hiv/.hivu/.rshot readers, the MCP filter expression parser) are exactly where this matters: a malformed input must return Err, never panic.

docs.title: Tests
docs.text:
New functionality in regshot-core should come with:

  • Unit tests for the specific behavior.
  • If it touches the diff engine: a property in tests/diff_properties.rs, or an argument for why the existing properties already cover it.

The HTML report's behavior lives in its embedded JavaScript, so changes there are tested in a real browser: crates/regshot-report/tests/html_browser.rs renders a report, loads it in headless Chromium (optionally with a deep-link hash, or with a script that simulates clicks and key presses), and asserts on the resulting DOM. Those tests find chromium/google-chrome on PATH, or the browser named by REGSHOT_TEST_BROWSER, and skip with a note when there's none. CI's Linux job has Chrome, so they always run there.

docs.title: Fuzzing
docs.text:
The parsers that read untrusted input have cargo-fuzz targets under fuzz/: .rshot reading, .hiv/.hivu import, the filter language, and regshot.ini migration. The two file-format targets also check that anything they accept survives a write-and-read-back round trip. They need a nightly toolchain and cargo-fuzz:

rustup toolchain install nightly
cargo install cargo-fuzz --locked
cd fuzz
cargo +nightly run --bin make-seeds           # valid starting inputs in corpus/
cargo +nightly fuzz run hive corpus/hive       # or rshot, filter, ini; Ctrl-C to stop

A crash leaves the input that caused it in fuzz/artifacts/<target>/, and cargo +nightly fuzz run <target> <that file> reproduces it. CI fuzzes each target for 30 seconds on every pull request, and for 10 minutes daily with a corpus that's kept between runs (.github/workflows/fuzz.yml). Touching one of these parsers usually deserves a longer local run than that.

docs.title: Docs
docs.text: If a change affects user-facing behavior, update the relevant page under docs/ in the same change — mkdocs build --strict runs in CI and fails on broken internal links, so a dangling reference is caught before merge.

docs.title: Where to start
docs.text: Check the changelog for what's implemented versus planned, and the repository issue tracker for open work. regshot-core's diff engine and data model are the most thoroughly tested part of the codebase and the best place to look for the project's actual conventions in practice.

docs.title: Translating
docs.text: regshot-rs shows its interface in your language: the GUI, the start menu, the explorer (regshot tui), command-line messages, and the txt and html reports. This page explains how the translations are organised, and how to fix one or add a language.

docs.title: What gets translated, and what doesn't
docs.text:
Translated Not translated GUI, start menu, explorer, help screens JSON, NDJSON/ECS, CSV, .reg, PowerShell, NSIS, Inno and .unl output txt and html reports .rshot files and anything else programs read Command-line messages people read: errors, progress, summaries --help, man pages and shell completions MCP tool descriptions (written for AI agents) Category codes (KEYADD, ValModi) and value types (REG_SZ)

Everything in the second column is an interface other programs depend on, so it stays the same in every language.

Error messages from deep inside regshot (for example, why a .rshot file couldn't be parsed) stay in English. The command-line message around them is translated, for example error: reading snapshot.rshot: ….
