docs.title: Choosing a language
docs.text:
regshot picks the first of these that is set:

  1. --lang de on the command line, or the REGSHOT_LANG environment variable.
  2. language = "de" under [ui] in the settings file. The GUI reads this too.
  3. Your system's language.
  4. English.

A regional tag falls back to its language. For example, de-AT uses German. auto means "use the system language".

docs.title: Where the text lives
docs.text:
Each language is one file, crates/regshot-i18n/locales/<tag>.ftl, in Fluent format. The files are built into the program, so nothing extra is installed. en.ftl is the source: every other file uses the same message IDs.

A message is an ID, =, and the text:

gui-button-open = Open snapshots…
tui-yanked = yanked: { $path }

{ $path } is a placeable, a value regshot fills in. Keep every placeable from the English message, spelled exactly the same. You can move it to wherever your language's word order needs it.

docs.title: Plurals
docs.text:
When a message depends on a number, it lists one form per plural category. English has two, one and other:

tui-all-triaged =
    { $count ->
        [one] the only row is triaged
       *[other] all { $count } rows are triaged
    }

Use your language's own categories. Russian uses one, few, many and other. Arabic uses zero, one, two, few, many and other. Japanese needs only other. The CLDR plural rules table lists them for every language. The variant marked with * is the fallback, and one variant must have it.

docs.title: Things to leave as they are
docs.text:
• Commands, flags and file names: `regshot export`, --view 64, .rshot, host:port.
  • Key names in brackets: [capture], [ui] language.
  • (NULL!), category codes, and value types.
  • The keyboard keys in the explorer's help (j/k, Ctrl-d). Only their descriptions are messages.

docs.title: Fixing or adding a translation
docs.text:
1. Edit crates/regshot-i18n/locales/<tag>.ftl. To add a language, copy en.ftl to <tag>.ftl, translate it, and add one line for it to LANGUAGES in crates/regshot-i18n/src/lib.rs: the tag, the language's name in itself, and whether it's written right to left.

  2. Check it:

    cargo test -p regshot-i18n

    This fails if a file doesn't parse, uses an ID English doesn't have, or uses different placeables from English. A message you leave out isn't an error: English is shown for it instead.

  3. Look at it: run cargo run -p regshot-cli -- --lang <tag> tui for the start menu, add tui a.rshot b.rshot for the explorer, or set [ui] language and start the GUI.

  4. For Chinese, Japanese or Korean, cargo test -p regshot-gui also checks that the GUI's bundled font has every character you used. If it fails, rebuild the fonts with crates/regshot-gui/assets/fonts/subset.sh (needs the GitHub CLI and fonttools).

Most of every translation is machine-generated, and each file's header says so. The exceptions are messages marked # imported: those come from upstream Regshot's language.ini, written by the people the header credits. Where an imported string was fixed (characters lost to an old codepage, a misspelling, a wrong word), the mark says # imported (corrected: …), and the test that checks imports against language.ini lists the same reason. Corrections from native speakers are very welcome.

docs.title: For developers: adding a message
docs.text:
• Show text with tr!("id"), or tr!("id", name = value) with arguments. Pass counts as numbers, not formatted strings, so plurals work.
  • Add the English message to en.ftl under the section for its surface. Prefixes: common-, gui-, menu-, tui-, cli-, report-.
  • Write whole sentences as one message. Don't build format!("{what} can't be empty") out of translated pieces, because word order differs between languages.
  • Pad terminal columns with regshot_i18n::pad_to or aligned_rows, not {:<N}. A Chinese or Japanese character is two columns wide.
  • cargo test -p regshot-i18n checks that every "id" in the sources exists in en.ftl, and that every message in en.ftl is used somewhere.
  • In the GUI, show translated text through the theme helpers (theme::label, theme::dim, theme::field and the buttons) or bidi::display, and data such as paths and labels through theme::data. They lay Hebrew and Arabic out right to left, which egui can't do itself. Arrange rows with theme::row and theme::trailing_row, so they mirror in those languages.
  • To see the result, cargo test -p regshot-gui --test screenshots -- --ignored renders the window in several languages to docs/images/gui/ (it needs a GPU, or Mesa's software renderer).

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
No published binaries yet

Release artifacts (v0.1.0 and later) will be attached to GitHub Releases for Windows x64, x86, and ARM64, plus a Linux x64 analysis-only build. Until then, build from source.

docs.title: Building from source
docs.text:
Requires Rust 1.88+ (edition 2024); rust-toolchain.toml in the repository pins the exact version CI uses.

git clone https://github.com/Tasty-Murder/regshot-rs.git
cd regshot-rs
cargo build --release --workspace

The regshot binary lands at target/release/regshot (.exe on Windows).

docs.title: Platform notes
docs.text:
Platform Capture Analysis Windows x64 Windows x86 (32-bit) planned Windows ARM64 planned Linux / macOS

Capture reads the live Windows registry and needs the real Win32 API; it cannot run on Linux/macOS. Analysis — loading and comparing .rshot files someone else captured — is platform-independent and works everywhere regshot-core compiles, which is why this project is developed primarily on Linux (see Architecture).

docs.title: Shell completions and man pages
docs.text:
Release archives include both, under completions/ and man/. They're generated from the same definition that parses the command line, so they always match the binary's flags. To make them yourself from any build:

regshot completion powershell > regshot-completion.ps1   # also: bash, zsh, fish, elvish
regshot man --out-dir ./man                               # regshot.1 plus one page per subcommand
Shell Install PowerShell . path\to\regshot-completion.ps1 in your $PROFILE bash source regshot.bash from ~/.bashrc, or copy it to /usr/share/bash-completion/completions/regshot zsh Put _regshot in a directory on your $fpath fish Copy regshot.fish to ~/.config/fish/completions/ elvish eval (slurp < regshot.elv) in rc.elv

docs.title: Verifying a release download
docs.text:
Every release asset ships alongside a .sha256 checksum file (see the release workflow). Verify with:

sha256sum -c regshot-rs-<version>-<target>.zip.sha256

docs.title: Just run regshot
docs.text:
With no command, regshot shows a menu of what it can do in the current folder:

  • open snapshots in the explorer;
  • take a snapshot (Windows);
  • compare snapshots into the HTML report;
  • export an undo script or installer;
  • import an upstream .hiv;
  • look at a snapshot's details;
  • reopen a snapshot set you've already triaged;
  • open the GUI or the settings file.

Nothing is loaded or run until you pick something. Each item shows the command it's equivalent to, so the menu is also a way to learn the commands below. When regshot isn't attached to a terminal (a script, CI, a pipe), it prints the help and exits with status 2 instead of waiting for input.

docs.title: The three-command loop
docs.text:
# Before: capture a baseline
regshot shot --out before.rshot --label "before install"

# … install the software, change a setting, whatever you're investigating …

# After: capture again
regshot shot --out after.rshot --label "after install"

# Compare, and open a self-contained HTML report
regshot diff before.rshot after.rshot --template html --out report.html --open

That's it for the classic two-shot case. The interesting part is that it isn't limited to two:

regshot shot --out s1.rshot --label "clean"
# … install …
regshot shot --out s2.rshot --label "after install"
# … reboot …
regshot shot --out s3.rshot --label "after reboot"

regshot diff s1.rshot s2.rshot s3.rshot --template html --out timeline.html --open

The report's timeline view shows one column per snapshot, so you can see when across the sequence a key appeared — not just that it eventually did.

docs.title: Filtering without a full report
docs.text:
regshot query s1.rshot s2.rshot --filter 'category == "VALADD" && path starts_with "HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run"'

See Filter syntax for the full expression grammar.

docs.title: Generating an undo script
docs.text:
regshot export before.rshot after.rshot --template ps1 --direction undo --out undo.ps1

See Undo scripts and installers — in particular, why .ps1 rather than .reg is the safe default when a diff spans both WOW64 views.

docs.title: CI usage
docs.text:
regshot diff uses exit codes 0 (no changes), 1 (changes found), 2 (error), so it's usable directly as a build-verification gate:

regshot diff before.rshot after.rshot --template json --out /dev/null || exit_code=$?
if [ "$exit_code" -eq 1 ]; then
  echo "registry changed during the build — investigate"
fi

docs.title: Automation
docs.text: The rule that keeps the CLI honest: it is complete on its own. Anything the TUI or a report template can do is reachable as a flag — that's what makes the tool usable in a sandbox, over WinRM, or from CI, rather than only interactively.

docs.title: Exit codes
docs.text: regshot diff uses 0 (no changes), 1 (changes found), 2 (error) — deliberately chosen so it works directly as a build-verification gate without wrapping it in a script that parses output.

docs.title: Machine-readable output
docs.text: Every command accepts --json for structured output, plus --quiet/--verbose and --no-color (honoring the NO_COLOR environment variable). regshot query --format ndjson streams one JSON object per line, suitable for piping into jq, a log shipper, or a SIEM ingestion pipeline (see also the ndjson-ecs output template).

docs.title: Shell completions and man pages
docs.text:
regshot completion zsh > _regshot

Generated via clap_complete; man pages via clap-mangen.

docs.title: Sandbox / malware-analysis automation
docs.text: The pattern: revert a VM to a clean snapshot, regshot shot, copy the sample in and run it, regshot shot again, regshot diff --template html --out report.html. The CLI plus the MCP server make this fully drivable by a script or an agent — no bespoke sandbox harness needed, just the three-command loop from the quickstart wrapped around whatever automates the "run the sample" step.

docs.title: Capturing
docs.text:
regshot shot --out snapshot.rshot [--view both|64|32] [--roots hklm,hku]
             [--whitelist-key <path>]... [--skip-key <path>]... [--label "…"]
             [--baseline before.rshot]

Capture reads each hive on every core and takes a few tens of seconds on a typical machine.

docs.title: Registry roots
docs.text: By default, capture scans HKLM and HKU — the same default as upstream Regshot. HKCU, HKCR, and HKCC are opt-in via --roots: HKCR in particular is enormous and mostly a merged view over HKLM\SOFTWARE\Classes and HKCU\SOFTWARE\Classes, so it's excluded by default.

docs.title: WOW64 views
docs.text: See Registry views for the full explanation. In short: --view both (the default on a 64-bit host) captures both the 64-bit and 32-bit views; --view 64 / --view 32 narrow to one.

docs.title: Skip and whitelist lists
docs.text:
• --skip-key <pattern> leaves out a key and everything under it. A skipped key isn't read at all, so skipping a large, noisy subtree also makes the capture faster.
  • --whitelist-key <pattern> is the inverse: when any whitelist entry is given, only those keys and everything under them are captured. This is the more effective tool once you know what you're watching. --whitelist-key 'HKLM\SOFTWARE\MyApp' captures a fast, tiny, focused snapshot instead of the entire registry.

Both take the same patterns, matched case-insensitively:

Pattern Matches HKLM\SOFTWARE\MyApp that key, in HKLM only. Long hive names (HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\…) work too SOFTWARE\MyApp that path under any hive, e.g. both HKLM\SOFTWARE\MyApp and a user's SOFTWARE\MyApp under HKU Temp every key named Temp, anywhere HKLM the whole hive

A pattern names whole keys: MyApp doesn't match MyAppX, and Temp doesn't match Attempt. When a key is both skipped and whitelisted, the skip wins.

docs.title: Incremental capture
docs.text:
The usual workflow is one snapshot before a change and one after. The second can reuse the first:

regshot shot --out before.rshot
# … install, configure, run something …
regshot shot --out after.rshot --baseline before.rshot

Windows records when each key was last written: whenever one of its values is set or deleted, or a subkey is created or deleted under it. With --baseline, a key whose time hasn't changed since the baseline gets the baseline's values instead of having them read again. Every key is still visited, since a change deeper down doesn't update its parents' times. The result is the same snapshot a full capture would produce, and regshot shot says how many keys it reused.

It's opt-in for one reason: a program can set a key's last write time to anything. Malware that changes a value and then sets the time back would go unnoticed. When you're investigating something that might do that, capture without --baseline.

The baseline must come from this machine and record key times. Snapshots from regshot-rs versions before key times were recorded, and .hiv imports, don't, so nothing is reused.

docs.title: Labels and metadata
docs.text: --label attaches a human-readable note ("before install") to the snapshot, shown in regshot info, the report, and the TUI. Every snapshot also records its capture timestamp, machine name, user, and the architecture/view set it was captured with — the last of which is what makes the registry-views safety check possible.

docs.title: What isn't captured
docs.text: regshot-rs is registry-only — no filesystem scanning, no file hashing. See No filesystem scanning for why, and what to use alongside it if you need the filesystem side too.

docs.title: Comparing
docs.text:
regshot diff s1.rshot s2.rshot [... sN.rshot] [--order ts|given] [--template html]
             [--out report.html] [--open] [--allow-view-mismatch] [--only-interesting]
             [--generalize | --no-generalize]

docs.title: N snapshots, not two
docs.text: Upstream Regshot compares exactly two shots. regshot-rs compares any number: pass two paths for the classic case, or a whole sequence — before, during, after, after-reboot — and get one timeline. Internally this is a single N-way merge-join over every snapshot's sorted key/value arrays (see Architecture), not a chain of pairwise diffs, so it's linear in the total number of entries regardless of how many snapshots you give it.

docs.title: Ordering
docs.text: --order ts (the default) sorts snapshots by their recorded capture timestamp before comparing, so transitions are always reported chronologically no matter what order you listed the files in. --order given uses the command-line order literally — useful when you're deliberately comparing out of chronological order, or when timestamps aren't trustworthy (e.g. clock skew across machines).

docs.title: Timeline vs. pairwise
docs.text:
The report and TUI offer two views over the same underlying data:

  • Timeline — one column per snapshot. The view that only makes sense with more than two snapshots: you see when across the sequence a key appeared, not just whether it eventually did.
  • Pairwise — the classic two-shot report, grouped by change category with counts, for any pair of snapshots in the set.

docs.title: View mismatches
docs.text: If the snapshots being compared were captured with different WOW64 view sets, every command that compares them refuses by default and names the mismatch. That covers diff, query, export and tui, and the MCP diff, suggest_interesting, query_changes, generate_report and export tools. Otherwise, comparing a 32-bit-view-only snapshot against a both-views one would read every 64-bit-only entry as a fabricated change. For export it's worse than misleading: the undo script would really delete every entry in the view only one side captured. Pass --allow-view-mismatch (allow_view_mismatch: true over MCP) if that's genuinely what you want, for example because one snapshot covers only the 32-bit view on purpose.

docs.title: The five change categories
docs.text:
Category Meaning KeyAdd A key present later that was absent before. KeyDel A key present before that is absent later. ValAdd A value present later that was absent before. ValDel A value present before that is absent later. ValModi A value present in both, with different data.

There is no KeyModi — a key carries no data of its own to modify, only its children do. See Change categories for the full reference, including how these interact with WOW64 views.

docs.title: Filtering noise
docs.text: A registry diff's signal is buried in noise — most of what changes during a normal session or install is uninteresting. regshot-rs has three complementary tools for cutting through it.

docs.title: Skip and whitelist lists
docs.text: The cheapest filter is deciding what to capture at all — see Capturing. --whitelist-key is the more effective tool once you know roughly where you're looking: with filesystem scanning out of scope (see No filesystem scanning), the whitelist is the primary noise control this tool has, not an optional extra.

docs.title: Path generalization
docs.text:
Filesystem paths that reach the registry as value data — ImagePath, Run entries, uninstall strings — are the part of a diff that actually matters for transferable indicators of compromise. regshot diff --generalize rewrites C:\Users\bob\AppData\Roaming\x.exe to %AppData%\x.exe (any drive letter, AppData\Local → %LocalAppData%) and collapses per-user SIDs under HKU\S-1-5-21-… to HKU\<user> — in the report only, never the underlying .rshot data, the same way --only-interesting only narrows what's already been rendered. Defaults to [report] generalize_paths in the config file (itself true by default); --no-generalize disables it even when the config file enables it.

REG_EXPAND_SZ values often already store the generalized form (that's what "expandable" means) — since the report renders them as readable text, --generalize applies to them the same way it does to REG_SZ, for the rarer case where one stores an absolute path instead. See Value rendering for how REG_EXPAND_SZ renders differently in the report than in a .reg export.

docs.title: Known-interesting heuristics
docs.text:
A curated table of high-interest locations — Run/RunOnce, services, scheduled tasks, AppInit_DLLs, Image File Execution Options, Winlogon, LSA packages, shell extensions — flags matching changes with a ⚠ badge and an "Only interesting" facet in the HTML report, in the suggest_interesting MCP tool (grouped findings, ranked by count), and with regshot diff --only-interesting (narrows the report and recomputes its summary counts to match).

Every entry is matched on (hive, path pattern) — deliberately not also on WOW64 view. A path under a redirected subtree (e.g. SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run) reads identically through both the 64-bit and 32-bit views; only the physical location differs. A rule that also required a specific view would miss every 32-bit installer's autorun entry entirely — the same aliasing bug the whole view-aware design exists to avoid, just showing up at the heuristics layer instead of the diff engine.

Per-user locations (the per-user Run keys and the rest) are listed under HKCU but also match under every user hive in HKU (HKU\S-1-5-21-…\Software\…, HKU\.DEFAULT\…). HKCU is only an alias for the signed-in user's HKU subtree, and captures default to HKLM + HKU, so that's where a per-user autorun actually appears. A pattern matches a key and the keys under it, never a sibling that merely shares its prefix, so …\RunOnce is labeled RunOnce, not Run.

This is one of the highest-value usability features after the timeline view itself, and nothing in the upstream Regshot lineage has it.

docs.title: GUI
docs.text:
regshot-gui is a small desktop window for managing snapshots and turning them into reports and scripts, for when you'd rather click than type. It's a shell over the same engine as the CLI: it doesn't browse diffs itself. Compare renders the HTML report and opens it in your browser, and the report is where you explore the changes. For a terminal-based explorer, use the TUI.

Everything the GUI does is also available from the CLI, so a workflow you start here can be scripted later.

docs.title: Snapshots
docs.text:
Open snapshots… loads .rshot files, and imports upstream Regshot .hiv/.hivu files directly (like regshot import-hive, but without writing a .rshot). The list shows each snapshot's label, capture time, WOW64 views, and size. Click a label for its details: file, computer, user, architecture, skipped entries, and the environment it recorded for expanding REG_EXPAND_SZ values.

The list order is the comparison order. Up, Down and Remove rearrange it, and Sort by capture time does what regshot diff --order ts does.

docs.title: Capturing (Windows)
docs.text:
Take snapshot… asks where to save the new .rshot, then captures in the background, showing how many keys and values it has scanned. When it finishes, the snapshot is loaded into the list. Because capture always writes a file first, a snapshot captured here is an ordinary .rshot that the CLI can use too. Capture settings holds the same options as regshot shot: label, views, hives, and skip and whitelist patterns (one per line). HKLM needs the GUI to run as Administrator.

Capture reads the Windows registry, so the button is disabled on other platforms, where the GUI still opens, compares and exports existing snapshots.

docs.title: Compare
docs.text:
Compare and open report… renders every loaded snapshot, in list order, into the HTML report, asks where to save it, and opens it. The checkboxes match regshot diff's flags:

  • Generalize per-user paths and SIDs: --generalize (on by default, as on the CLI).
  • Only known-interesting locations: --only-interesting.
  • Allow view mismatch: --allow-view-mismatch. Without it, snapshots captured with different view sets are refused, exactly as the CLI refuses them. See View mismatches.

docs.title: Export
docs.text: Pick a from and to snapshot, a template (ps1, reg5, reg4, nsis, inno, unl), a direction and optionally a single view. Export… then writes the file with the right encoding for its reader. It's the same rendering as regshot export, including its refusals: a .reg changeset spanning both views needs a view picked, and data a format can't express exactly is listed rather than dropped. The export is checked before the save dialog opens, so a refusal never costs you a dialog. The Allow view mismatch checkbox applies here too.

docs.title: Appearance
docs.text: The window looks the same on Windows and Linux: it brings its own fonts (Inter for text, JetBrains Mono for paths and values) and icons rather than using each system's. It uses the same logo-derived palette as the HTML report, in light or dark following your system setting.

docs.title: Languages
docs.text:
The GUI shows the language set by --lang, [ui] language in the settings file, or your system, like the rest of regshot-rs (see Translating). It bundles fonts for Chinese, Japanese and Korean, so those languages work without any fonts installed.

Hebrew and Arabic are drawn right to left, and the whole window mirrors: the snapshot list moves to the right, and labels, rows and buttons start from the right. Paths, numbers and other left-to-right text inside a sentence keep their own direction.

One gap remains: right-to-left text typed into a text field, such as a capture label, shows its words in the order you typed them. The text itself is stored correctly, and shows right everywhere else.

docs.title: Settings
docs.text:
The GUI starts from the same settings file as the CLI:

  • [capture] fills in the capture settings (hives, views, and skip and whitelist patterns).
  • [report] generalize_paths sets whether Generalize per-user paths and SIDs starts ticked.

Changing a setting in the window affects only that session. If the file can't be read, or holds a value the GUI doesn't recognize, the status bar says so and the built-in default is used instead.

docs.title: MCP server
docs.text:
Read this before enabling HTTP

The MCP server can take registry snapshots of the running machine — that's a high-privilege capability to expose over a network, even to localhost. Read the security model below before you enable the HTTP transport, not after.

regshot mcp                                  # stdio (default)
regshot mcp --http 127.0.0.1:7777            # streamable HTTP, loopback-only unless overridden
regshot mcp --http 127.0.0.1:7777 --allow-capture --no-auth   # loopback only; --no-auth refused otherwise

docs.title: Status
docs.text:
Implemented: both transports, and every tool below, including take_snapshot (Windows-only, gated behind --allow-capture; on any other platform it returns a clear error instead of attempting a capture). load_snapshot isn't in the table below — it's how a session gets a .rshot file into memory at all before the other tools have anything to work with, which the table's original design didn't spell out as its own tool.

Each MCP session (from initialize onward, identified by the Mcp-Session-Id the server assigns) gets its own fresh, isolated set of loaded snapshots — nothing is shared across clients, the same way a new stdio process would have nothing shared with any other.

docs.title: Why this exists
docs.text:
A diff can be a million rows — far more than an agent's context can hold — so the tool surface is built around aggregation, never dumping: diff returns category counts only; query_changes is the workhorse, a filter expression plus optional group-by that answers "what did this install touch under Run?" without flooding the model with rows it didn't ask for.

This makes a genuinely new workflow possible: an agent can be told "install this MSI and tell me what it changed," and run take_snapshot → (install) → take_snapshot → diff → suggest_interesting → query_changes on the flagged areas → export an undo script, entirely on its own. Registry-only scope helps here, not hurts: a filesystem diff of an installer is tens of thousands of rows of unpacked payload; the registry diff is the part that says what the software actually did to the system, and it's small enough for an agent to reason about.

docs.title: Tools
docs.text: Tool Returns load_snapshot Loads an existing .rshot file into the session. Id + counts. take_snapshot Snapshot id + counts. Requires --allow-capture; Windows-only. list_snapshots Ids, labels, timestamps, machine, counts diff Summary only — counts per category per transition query_changes Filter expression + optional aggregation — the workhorse get_value_data One value's data: readable text, raw hex, and (for REG_EXPAND_SZ) its expanded form describe_filter_syntax The filter vocabulary — self-teaching generate_report Writes the file, returns the path (not the content) export Returns undo/redo script text (reg4/reg5/ps1/unl), or an installer + uninstaller script (nsis/inno) suggest_interesting Ranked findings from the known-interesting heuristics, grouped by rule with counts

docs.title: Connecting a client
docs.text:
In stdio mode (the default), your agent starts regshot mcp itself and talks to it over stdin/stdout, so you don't start or daemonize anything. Register it once:

claude mcp add regshot -- regshot mcp        # Claude Code
codex mcp add regshot -- regshot mcp         # Codex

The README has config examples for opencode, Cursor, VS Code, Gemini CLI, and the HTTP transport. Run by hand in a terminal, regshot mcp prints those registration commands and waits. Ctrl-C or Ctrl-D exits cleanly.

docs.title: Running regshot as a background service
docs.text:
Most people don't need this. If your agent starts regshot mcp itself (the stdio setup above), it runs only while the agent needs it, and there's nothing to keep running.

You need a service only when you use the HTTP transport (regshot mcp --http …). With HTTP, you start the server and the agent connects to it. Typically that's because the agent runs somewhere it can't start Windows programs, such as WSL, a container or a VM. Without a service, you'd have to keep a terminal open with the server running in it. A service starts it for you in the background, with no window, every time the computer starts.

docs.title: Windows: a Task Scheduler task
docs.text:
Windows' built-in Task Scheduler can start a program at boot and keep it running. Open PowerShell as Administrator (right-click → Run as administrator) and run these steps in order.

1. Create the task. Change $exe if you installed regshot somewhere else. Run (Get-Command regshot).Source to find where it is.

$exe       = "C:\Program Files\regshot-rs\regshot.exe"
$action    = New-ScheduledTaskAction -Execute $exe -Argument "mcp --http 127.0.0.1:7777"
$trigger   = New-ScheduledTaskTrigger -AtStartup
$principal = New-ScheduledTaskPrincipal -UserId "$env:USERDOMAIN\$env:USERNAME" -LogonType S4U
$settings  = New-ScheduledTaskSettingsSet -ExecutionTimeLimit ([TimeSpan]::Zero) `
                 -RestartCount 3 -RestartInterval (New-TimeSpan -Minutes 1)
Register-ScheduledTask -TaskName "regshot-mcp" -Action $action -Trigger $trigger `
    -Principal $principal -Settings $settings

What each part does:

  • -AtStartup starts the server when Windows boots, before anyone logs in.
  • -LogonType S4U runs it as you, but without saving your password and without a window. (S4U stands for "Service for User".) Because it runs as you, it uses your token file. The one limit is that it can't reach network shares or EFS-encrypted files, which regshot doesn't need.
  • -ExecutionTimeLimit ([TimeSpan]::Zero) removes Task Scheduler's default rule of stopping a task after 72 hours.
  • -RestartCount 3 -RestartInterval … tells Task Scheduler to try starting it again, up to 3 times, if it ever fails.

To let the agent take live snapshots too, add --allow-capture after mcp in -Argument, and add -RunLevel Highest to the New-ScheduledTaskPrincipal line. Reading HKLM needs administrator rights. Read the security model before doing this.

2. Start it now, instead of waiting for the next reboot:

Start-ScheduledTask -TaskName "regshot-mcp"

3. Check that it's running. This asks the server to start an MCP session with your token:

$token = Get-Content "$env:APPDATA\regshot\mcp-token"
Invoke-WebRequest http://127.0.0.1:7777/mcp -Method Post -ContentType "application/json" `
    -Headers @{ Authorization = "Bearer $token"; Accept = "application/json, text/event-stream" } `
    -Body '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":1,"method":"initialize","params":{"protocolVersion":"2025-06-18","capabilities":{},"clientInfo":{"name":"check","version":"0"}}}'
Result Meaning StatusCode : 200 Running, and your token works. (401) Unauthorized Running, but that isn't the token it uses. "Unable to connect" Not running. See below.

If it isn't running, Get-ScheduledTaskInfo -TaskName "regshot-mcp" shows when it last ran and its LastTaskResult. 0 means it exited normally; anything else is an error code.

4. Connect your agent with the URL http://127.0.0.1:7777/mcp and the token from step 3. The README has the config for each agent.

Stop it or remove it:

Stop-ScheduledTask       -TaskName "regshot-mcp"                   # stop until next boot
Disable-ScheduledTask    -TaskName "regshot-mcp"                   # stop starting at boot
Unregister-ScheduledTask -TaskName "regshot-mcp" -Confirm:$false   # delete the task

Why not a \"real\" Windows service?

Windows services (the ones sc.exe create or services.msc manage) have to be written to talk to the Service Control Manager, and regshot isn't. sc.exe create would accept it, but starting it fails with error 1053: the service did not respond in a timely fashion. Task Scheduler runs ordinary programs, so it does the same job here without that.

docs.title: Linux: a systemd user service
docs.text:
Live capture is Windows-only, so on Linux the server can only analyse existing .rshot files. systemd, the program that starts services on most Linux systems, can run it for your user account.

1. Create the file ~/.config/systemd/user/regshot-mcp.service. Change the ExecStart path if which regshot shows a different one:

[Unit]
Description=regshot-rs MCP server (streamable HTTP)

[Service]
ExecStart=%h/.cargo/bin/regshot mcp --http 127.0.0.1:7777
Restart=on-failure

[Install]
WantedBy=default.target

2. Start it now and at every login:

systemctl --user daemon-reload
systemctl --user enable --now regshot-mcp

3. Optional: keep it running when you're logged out. By default, systemd stops your user services when you log out and starts them at your next login. To run it from boot regardless:

loginctl enable-linger

4. Check it and get the token:

systemctl --user status regshot-mcp      # should say "active (running)"
cat ~/.config/regshot/mcp-token          # the token to give your agent

To stop it, run systemctl --user stop regshot-mcp. To remove it, run systemctl --user disable --now regshot-mcp and delete the file.

docs.title: Security model
docs.text:
Control Default Transport stdio — no network surface at all. HTTP (--http host:port) is opt-in. Bind address Must be loopback (127.0.0.1/::1) unless --allow-non-loopback is passed, which also prints a loud warning at startup — this flag adds no firewall or reverse proxy of its own. Host header Validated against an allowlist (localhost, 127.0.0.1, [::1], plus the concrete bind address) — mismatch is rejected with 403. This is rmcp's own DNS-rebinding mitigation. Authentication A bearer token is generated on first run, persisted at the platform config directory (…/regshot/mcp-token, 0600 on Unix) so it survives restarts, and printed to stderr at every startup. Required unless --no-auth is passed, and --no-auth is itself refused on a non-loopback bind. Capture tools Gated behind --allow-capture. Without it, the server can analyse existing snapshots but cannot touch the live registry — the natural mode for an analysis workstation. Write scope No tool writes to the registry. Undo/redo scripts are returned as text, never executed.

The concrete threat this defends against: browser-based DNS rebinding against local MCP servers is a documented, real vulnerability class (CVE-2025-66414 affected every HTTP-based MCP server built on an unpatched SDK) — the browser's same-origin check happens before DNS resolution, so "it's only listening on localhost" is not, by itself, a security boundary. That's why the Host check exists even though the bind address is loopback-only by default.

docs.title: Output templates
docs.text:
Every output format — the HTML report, plain text, .reg scripts, PowerShell undo scripts, installer scripts, JSON — is driven by the same template engine rather than hand-coded per format. This is the idea Regshot-Advanced got right, generalized: formats are data, described by a small manifest plus a minijinja template rather than an ad-hoc INI dialect.

regshot templates --list            # every built-in and on-disk template
regshot templates --show reg5       # inspect one template's manifest and body

docs.title: Built-in templates
docs.text: Template Output Notes txt Plain text Byte-comparable with upstream 1.9.1's output, for existing scripts html The interactive report Special-cased: data-embedding, not line-templated json Structured timeline For tooling ndjson-ecs One ECS-shaped event per change SIEM ingestion reg4 / reg5 REGEDIT4 (ANSI) / Windows Registry Editor Version 5.00 .reg Undo or redo — see the direction flag below ps1 PowerShell undo/redo The default for undo export — see why nsis / inno Installer + uninstaller script, registry sections only "Diff an install, get the registry half of an installer" unl Line-parsable format Regshot-Advanced compatibility

docs.title: Direction: undo vs. redo
docs.text: Direction is a parameter, not a separate template — --direction undo reverses each transition, --direction redo replays it. One template covers what Regshot-Advanced needed two templates (installer and uninstaller) for. The installer templates (nsis/inno) go one step further and carry both directions in one script: --direction picks what the installer does (default redo), and the generated uninstaller always does the opposite. Every other template defaults to undo.

docs.title: Writing your own template
docs.text:
A template is a TOML manifest plus a Jinja body:

# templates/reg5.toml
name        = "reg5"
extension   = ".reg"
encoding    = "utf-16le"
bom         = true
group_keys  = true              # group values under one [key] header — required for valid .reg
entity_kinds = ["key", "value"] # skip anything not registry-shaped

[escapes.name]
'\' = '\\'
'"' = '\"'

[body]
template = "reg5.j2"

Escaping is tested, not hoped: every built-in template's escape table is checked against a fixture suite, and a generated .reg is round-tripped through a parser in tests to prove it is actually valid — a wrong .reg file is a live-system risk, not a cosmetic bug.

docs.title: Reading the report
docs.text: The HTML report is a single self-contained file — inline CSS and JS, zero network requests, built for isolated analysis machines. It's designed to stay usable at real-world scale: a full registry diff routinely produces 100k–1M rows, so the report virtualizes rendering (only the rows actually visible in the viewport are ever materialized as DOM nodes) rather than choking the browser.

docs.title: Layout
docs.text:
┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  regshot-rs · <label>            [Timeline ▸ Pairwise]   [⌕ search] │
├──────────────┬─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ SNAPSHOTS    │  Cat  Kind  View  Path                        Name   │
│ [0] before   │   ~   value  64   HKLM\…\Run\Updater           …     │
│ [1] after    │   +   key    32   HKLM\…\CurrentVersion\…            │
│              │                                                      │
│ FILTERS      │                                                      │
│ ☑ Keys       │                                                      │
│ ☑ Values     ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ CATEGORY     │  Path      HKLM\SOFTWARE\…\Run\Updater                │
│ ☑ KeyAdd 3   │  Category  VALMODI                                   │
│ ☑ ValModi 12 │  S2        "C:\ProgramData\upd.exe"                  │
│ VIEW         │  S3        "C:\ProgramData\upd.exe --silent"         │
│ ☑ 64  ☑ 32   │  (differing text highlighted)                        │
└──────────────┴─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
  • Timeline / pairwise toggle — see Comparing. Timeline reconstructs each entity's presence across every compared snapshot (not just consecutive pairs) entirely client-side from the same flat change list the pairwise view uses — no extra data needed.
  • Detail panel — click (or arrow-key to) a row to see its full path, category, and — for a value row — the rendered data on each side of the change, with the differing prefix/suffix highlighted. This is a bottom panel, not an inline expansion, so it doesn't complicate the fixed-height row math virtualization depends on.
  • View facet — filter to the 64-bit view, the 32-bit view, native, or unknown; see Registry views.
  • Search, facets, keyboard nav — instant client-side substring search over path and value name, facets by kind/category/view, and j/k/g/G///Esc navigation.
  • ⚠ Known-interesting — a ⚠ badge on any row matching the known-interesting-location heuristics (Run, Services, AppInit_DLLs, …), an "Only interesting" facet, and the matched rule name shown in the detail panel.
  • Deep links — see below.

docs.title: Deep links
docs.text:
The URL's #hash always mirrors what you're looking at: timeline or pairwise, the search text, any facet you've turned off, and the selected row. Copy link copies it, and opening that link (or pasting a new hash into a report that's already open) restores exactly that view, with the selected row scrolled into sight and its detail panel open. The hash updates in place as you move around, so j/k and typing don't fill your back-button history.

A link is identified by the row itself — its view, path, and value name, plus which transition in pairwise mode — not by its position, so it still points at the same change if you open it with different filters. A link to a row that isn't in the report just opens with nothing selected.

The link is the report file's own path plus the hash, so it only works for someone who has the same report file. Nothing about the view is sent anywhere, and opening a link still makes no network requests. The same goes for the selection generally: changing a filter keeps the selected row selected, or clears the selection if that row is filtered out, instead of jumping to whatever row now sits in the same position.

Hash key Meaning m=p Pairwise mode (timeline is the default) q= Search text kind=, cat=, view= The facet values still enabled, comma-separated (present only when some are off) int=1 Only known-interesting rows sv=, sp=, sn= Selected row's view, path, and value name (sn absent for a key row, empty for a key's default value) at=<from>-<to> Selected row's transition, in pairwise mode

docs.title: Visual design
docs.text:
The report's colors are a deliberate tribute to the original Regshot icon: black and white carry the layout, and the three logo-derived hues — blue, red, green — carry meaning only, never chrome. Every accent is contrast-checked against its own background (light and dark themes use different tints of the same hue, since the icon's raw blue fails contrast on white):

Role Light theme Dark theme Accent / modified #0B6AAE #56B6F8 (the icon's own blue) Added #1F7A34 #5DD17A Deleted #B81919 #FF6B6B

Color is never the only signal — every change also carries a glyph (+/−/~) and a distinct row treatment, since roughly 8% of men have a red/green color vision deficiency and a red/green diff is precisely the worst case for it.

docs.title: Value rendering
docs.text:
REG_SZ/REG_EXPAND_SZ render as "…" and REG_DWORD as dword:…, and the detail panel highlights the differing prefix/suffix of that text between the two sides. Everything else (binary, REG_QWORD, REG_MULTI_SZ, REG_NONE, …) is a hex(N):… byte list, which the detail panel shows as a classic hex dump: offset, 16 bytes per line in hex, and the same bytes as ASCII. Every byte that differs from the same offset on the other side, including bytes one side has and the other doesn't, is marked in both columns. The dump stops after the first 4096 bytes and says how many more there are.

Each side also shows its size in bytes. A value that exists but holds zero bytes shows upstream Regshot's (NULL!), which is different from (absent), a value that doesn't exist at that point. It's also different from an empty REG_SZ: that still holds its 2-byte NUL terminator, so it shows as "" with a size of 2. The JSON output carries the same sizes as from_size/to_size.

REG_EXPAND_SZ renders as readable text here — genuinely different from what a reg4/reg5 export writes for the same value (hex(2):…, matching real regedit.exe's own .reg-export behavior, since the quoted-string syntax has no way to mark a value as expandable). A report is for reading, an export file is for reg.exe to import; each renders the value the way its own reader needs.

Under a REG_EXPAND_SZ value, the detail panel also shows its expanded form, with every %VAR% resolved the way Windows' ExpandEnvironmentStrings would have resolved it on the captured machine. The values come from the environment the snapshot recorded at capture, not from the machine viewing the report. A variable that wasn't set at capture stays as %NAME%, as Windows leaves it, and is listed under "not set at capture". Snapshots written before environment recording existed, and legacy .hiv imports, have nothing to expand against, so they show only the stored form. --generalize applies to the expanded text too, because expanding %AppData% brings back the per-user path it exists to hide. The JSON output carries the same data as from_expanded/to_expanded, and the TUI's detail pane shows it too.

docs.title: Registry views (WOW64)
docs.text: This page explains the single most important correctness detail in regshot-rs, and the reason RegView exists as a first-class concept rather than an afterthought.

docs.title: The problem
docs.text:
On 64-bit Windows the registry has two views. A 32-bit process reading HKLM\SOFTWARE\Foo is transparently redirected by the WOW64 registry redirector to the physical location HKLM\SOFTWARE\Wow6432Node\Foo. Microsoft's own documentation is explicit that this is invisible to the application — no error, no warning, no indication.

The consequence for a snapshot differ is severe and silent: a 32-bit build and a 64-bit build of the same tool, run on the same machine at the same moment, capture different registries at the same path. Diff one against the other and every 64-bit-only key reads as deleted and every 32-bit-only key reads as added — a completely fabricated changeset, and nothing in either snapshot says so.

docs.title: The rules regshot-rs follows
docs.text:
1. Always specify the view explicitly. Every registry open carries either KEY_WOW64_64KEY or KEY_WOW64_32KEY — never neither, which would silently inherit process bitness.
  2. Never hard-code Wow6432Node. The physical redirection target is a Windows implementation detail Microsoft explicitly reserves the right to change — and already has: on Windows on ARM, 32-bit ARM apps redirect to WowAA32Node, not Wow6432Node. regshot-rs excludes the redirection node by which view-flagged handle is open, never by matching a literal path segment.
  3. Both views are captured by default on a 64-bit host. --view 64 / --view 32 narrow to one view when you know that's what you want (e.g. matching what a specific 32-bit application sees).

docs.title: How it's modeled
docs.text:
Every interned path is rooted under a RegView (Native, Wow64_64, Wow64_32, or Unknown for imported legacy snapshots). Two paths with identical text but different views intern to different ids and can never accidentally match during a diff — the fabricated-changeset bug above is prevented at the type level, not by a runtime check someone could forget to call.

SnapMeta records which view(s) a snapshot contains. Every command that compares snapshots (diff, query, export, tui, and the MCP tools that compare) refuses snapshots whose captured view sets differ. The error names the mismatch, and --allow-view-mismatch overrides it explicitly. See View mismatches.

docs.title: Reports and exports are view-aware too
docs.text:
• The HTML report and TUI both facet on view, and a 32-bit-view row carries a 32 badge inline so a screenshot is unambiguous.
  • .reg files have no syntax for expressing a WOW64 view — importing one as a 64-bit process always writes the 64-bit view, regardless of where the change was originally observed. So regshot export --template reg5 refuses a changeset that spans both views (pass --view to pick one), while --template ps1 opens keys through an explicit [Microsoft.Win32.RegistryView] and handles a mixed-view changeset natively — which is why PowerShell, not .reg, is the default export format.

docs.title: Practical guidance
docs.text:
• On 64-bit Windows, prefer the x64 build of regshot even when investigating 32-bit software: it captures both views by default, so nothing is missed.
  • If you specifically want to see the registry the way a particular 32-bit process sees it, use --view 32.
  • A legacy .hiv/.hivu import has no view information (upstream predates this distinction) and is tagged Unknown — comparing it against a natively-captured snapshot produces a warning for the same underlying reason.

docs.title: TUI
docs.text:
regshot tui                                                          # start menu
regshot tui before.rshot after.rshot [more.rshot …] [--allow-view-mismatch]   # explorer

Run with no snapshots, regshot tui opens a start menu over the working directory. It can open snapshots found there in the explorer, take a snapshot (Windows), compare to an HTML report, export an undo script or installer, import an upstream .hiv, show a snapshot's details, reopen a triaged set, or open the GUI or the settings file. Nothing loads until you choose, and each item shows the command it's equivalent to. With no terminal attached it prints its help and exits 2 instead of waiting for input.

Given snapshots, it opens straight into the explorer described below.

An interactive terminal explorer over the same diff engine as the HTML report, for working through a large diff without leaving the terminal. Every snapshot you pass is loaded at once. As everywhere else, snapshots captured with different WOW64 view sets are refused unless you pass --allow-view-mismatch.

docs.title: Pairwise and timeline
docs.text:

  • Pairwise (the default) lists what changed between the F and T snapshots, which start out as the last two.
  • Timeline lists everything that changed anywhere across all the loaded snapshots, with a states column holding one character per snapshot: + it appeared there, − it was removed, ~ its value changed, ● present and unchanged, blank absent. docs.title: Search
docs.text: / searches fuzzily, using the same matcher as the Helix editor: the characters you type have to appear in order in a row's path and value name, but not next to each other, so runupd finds …\CurrentVersion\Run\Updater. Matching ignores case. Search doesn't hide rows; it moves the selection. n/N step through the matches best first, where matches at the start of a path segment and longer unbroken runs rank higher. The search runs over the rows the table currently shows, so a category filter or a mode switch changes what it can find.

docs.title: Triage marking
docs.text:
For a 100k-row registry diff, marking rows reviewed is more valuable than it is for a code review: work through the noise once, mark it, and V jumps to the next unexamined change (wrapping around). The facets pane counts how much of the current pair is triaged. X clears every mark, but only on a second X, and any other key cancels.

Marks are saved as you make them, in a .regshot-triage-<hash>.json file next to the first snapshot. The hash covers the contents of every snapshot, in order, so reopening the TUI on the same snapshots brings the marks back, while a different set or a different order starts clean. The file disappears once nothing is marked. A mark records the change's view, path and value name, matched case-insensitively like the registry itself.

regshot query <snapshots…> --triaged only|exclude reads the same file, listing just the changes you've marked, or just the ones you haven't looked at yet.

docs.title: Performance
docs.text: Real diffs have 100k–1M rows. The table holds only indexes into the timeline, not rendered rows, and each frame builds widgets just for the rows that fit on screen. Frame cost therefore depends on the terminal's size, not the diff's.

docs.title: Testing
docs.text: The TUI renders through ratatui's test backend in the crate's tests, so every layout change is checked with insta frame snapshots on Linux. That's where the picture above comes from.

docs.title: Undo scripts and installers
docs.text: regshot export from.rshot to.rshot --template ps1 --direction undo --out undo.ps1

docs.title: Why PowerShell is the default, not .reg
docs.text:
A .reg file has no syntax for expressing a WOW64 view. Importing one as a 64-bit process always writes the 64-bit view, regardless of where the original change was observed — so an undo script generated from a diff that touched the 32-bit view would silently write to the wrong place if exported as .reg.

Because of that:

  • --template reg4 / --template reg5 refuse a changeset that spans both views, and require --view to pick one explicitly. The emitted file carries a header comment naming the view and the reg.exe /reg:32 / /reg:64 invocation needed to import it correctly.
  • --template ps1 opens keys through an explicit [Microsoft.Win32.RegistryKey]::OpenBaseKey(..., [Microsoft.Win32.RegistryView]::Registry32) and handles a mixed-view changeset natively — which is why it's the default for undo export.

docs.title: reg4 vs. reg5
docs.text: reg5 (Windows Registry Editor Version 5.00) is Unicode — UTF-16LE with a BOM, no encoding limits on key/value names or string data. reg4 (REGEDIT4) predates that: it's upstream Regshot's own export format, single-byte ANSI text with no BOM. Every value type renders identically between the two except REG_SZ text outside Latin-1 (ISO-8859-1) — reg4 falls back to hex(1): with the raw UTF-16LE bytes rather than losing data to ? replacement, which is lossless on any NT-based Windows (every target this project supports): a hex(N): byte list is imported as raw bytes verbatim regardless of which format header wrote the file, and REG_SZ is always stored internally as UTF-16LE either way — only the quoted-string syntax is codepage-limited, not the hex form. Key/value names have no such fallback (there's no hex escape for a name in .reg syntax), so a name outside Latin-1 genuinely is replaced with ? — reg4's one unavoidable, lossy case.

docs.title: The correctness bar
docs.text: Undo output is used to revert changes on a live system. A wrong script is not a cosmetic bug. Every undo/redo template is covered by a property test that reconstructs the "from" snapshot's key/value identity set starting from the "to" snapshot and the generated diff alone, and asserts it matches the actual "from" snapshot exactly — undo(diff(s1, s2)) applied to s2 must equal s1. This is the property that justifies calling the output an "undo" script at all, and it's checked against thousands of generated inputs, not a handful of examples.

docs.title: Installer script generation
docs.text:
regshot export before.rshot after.rshot --template nsis --out setup.nsi
regshot export before.rshot after.rshot --template inno --out setup.iss

--template nsis / --template inno produce an installer and uninstaller pair covering the registry side of "diff an install, get an installer." This is narrower than what Regshot-Advanced can do with its filesystem tracking (there's no copied-files section, since regshot-rs doesn't see the filesystem — see No filesystem scanning), but the registry half is often the part that actually needs reproducing.

One script carries both halves: the installer replays the captured changes and the uninstaller reverts them. --direction undo swaps the two, for an "installer" whose job is to roll a machine back. The installer name, output file name and default install directory come from the --out file's name. Neither installer registers itself in Add/Remove Programs, since that entry would itself be a registry change outside the captured diff. The uninstaller sits in the install directory instead (uninstall.exe for NSIS, unins000.exe for Inno).

nsis inno Needs NSIS 3.02+ (makensis) Inno Setup 6.3+ (ISCC) Install side WriteReg* / DeleteReg* instructions [Registry] entries Uninstall side Section "Uninstall", same instructions generated [Code] run at uninstall WOW64 view SetRegView 64/32 before each run of same-view entries HKLM64/HKLM32-style roots per entry Mixed-view changeset ✅ ✅

Both handle a changeset spanning both WOW64 views natively, unlike .reg. Entries captured under the native view follow the installer's own 64-bit handling, which means the 64-bit view on 64-bit Windows and the only view on 32-bit Windows. A changeset that touches an explicit 64-bit or 32-bit view refuses to run on 32-bit Windows, where those views don't exist.

docs.title: What each format can't express
docs.text:
The correctness bar above applies here too. If any entry can't be written exactly, export fails and lists the offending entries rather than emitting a script with gaps. ps1 can express everything and is the fallback.

  • NSIS has no instruction for REG_QWORD, REG_DWORD_BIG_ENDIAN, REG_LINK, or resource lists. It can't write a string with an embedded NUL or a control character other than CR, LF and tab. A default NSIS build truncates strings past 1023 characters, makensis rejects binary data over 3072 bytes, and WriteRegMultiStr requires double-NUL-terminated data.
  • Inno's [Registry] section (the install side) has no ValueType for REG_NONE, big-endian DWORDs, links, or resource lists. Each entry is a single line, so it can't carry a string containing a line break, and it can't write a multi-string with empty items.
  • Inno's uninstaller has no such limits. It restores every value byte-for-byte by calling RegSetValueExW directly. Inno's own RegWriteBinaryValue passes binary data through the system's ANSI codepage and would silently corrupt any byte ≥ 0x80. Anything it fails to revert is logged and reported when the uninstaller finishes, never skipped silently.

Every run of Windows CI compiles both formats with the real toolchains and runs the installer and uninstaller against a live registry in both views. It asserts that the registry ends up exactly in the captured "after" state, then exactly back in the "before" state.

docs.title: unl: Regshot-Advanced's removal list
docs.text: --template unl writes Regshot-Advanced's line-parsable format: a Title=/Log=1 header, then one live Registry="HKLM\…" (key) or Registry="HKLM\…","name" (value) line per entry to remove. Writes appear as ;-commented lines, with the data in .reg literal syntax, so the file still documents the whole changeset. A key's default value is written as {Standard}, matching Advanced. Like .reg, unl has no syntax for a WOW64 view, so a mixed-view changeset needs --view. It defaults to --direction undo, which lists what reverting the change would remove.

docs.title: Change categories
docs.text:
Five categories, all derived from a presence/hash transition crossed with entity kind — never stored directly, always computed from two states.

Category Badge Meaning KeyAdd KeyAdd A key present later that was absent before. KeyDel KeyDel A key present before that is absent later. ValAdd ValAdd A value present later that was absent before. ValDel ValDel A value present before that is absent later. ValModi ValModi A value present in both, with different data.

There is no KeyModi: a key carries no data of its own, only its children do, so "present in both" for a key is never a change on its own.

docs.title: Categories are disjoint and exhaustive
docs.text: For any entity and any pair of snapshots, exactly one category applies, or none (unchanged). This is one of the properties checked by property-based testing against thousands of generated snapshot pairs, not just a design intent.

docs.title: Interaction with WOW64 views
docs.text: Category derivation happens after entity identity is resolved, and identity includes the WOW64 view a key/value was captured under. A key that exists in both the 64-bit and 32-bit views at the same textual path is two different entities, each independently eligible for its own category — never merged, never treated as "the same key."

regshot config --init                    # write a default TOML config

docs.title: TOML, not INI
docs.text:
Upstream Regshot's regshot.ini is replaced with a TOML config, with a migration reader for existing .ini files. Filesystem-related keys in an imported .ini (ScanDir1, SkipDir, …) produce a warning naming each one as ignored, rather than being silently dropped — regshot-rs is registry-only.

Both the CLI and the GUI read this file as defaults. On the command line, a flag you pass always wins over the file.

docs.title: Where it lives
docs.text: The standard per-platform config directory: %APPDATA%\regshot\config.toml on Windows, ~/.config/regshot/config.toml on Linux/macOS.

docs.title: Shape
docs.text:
[capture]
roots = ["hklm", "hku"]
view = "both"
skip_key = []
whitelist_key = []

[report]
default_template = "html"
generalize_paths = true

[mcp]
allow_capture = false

[ui]
language = ""

regshot config --init/--migrate write exactly this shape. Every command that has a matching flag reads this file back in as its default — a CLI flag always wins when given:

Config key Command default for Merge with the CLI flag capture.roots shot --roots CLI value used if given, else this list capture.view shot --view CLI value used if given, else this value capture.skip_key shot --skip-key CLI list used if non-empty, else this list capture.whitelist_key shot --whitelist-key CLI list used if non-empty, else this list report.default_template diff --template CLI value used if given, else this value report.generalize_paths diff --generalize/--no-generalize Either explicit flag wins; else this value mcp.allow_capture mcp --allow-capture OR'd together — either one enables it ui.language --lang (every command), and the GUI's language CLI value used if given, else this value; empty or auto follows the system

mcp.allow_capture is OR'd rather than "CLI overrides config" like the others: --allow-capture is a bare enable switch with no --no-allow-capture counterpart, so there's no flag that could force capture off when the config file already turns it on. generalize_paths doesn't have this problem — --generalize/--no-generalize are a proper negatable pair — which is why it defaults to true: path generalization is meant to be on unless a specific diff needs the real, unrewritten paths.

docs.text: Used by regshot query and the MCP query_changes tool. The vocabulary is intentionally small and self-teaching — regshot query --help and the MCP describe_filter_syntax tool both emit this same reference.

docs.title: Why a filter language and not just flags
docs.text: A diff can be a million rows. regshot query/query_changes exist so one expression answers "what did this install write under Run?" without ever materializing the full row set — the same reason the MCP diff tool returns category counts only and leaves drilling in to this filter.

docs.title: .rshot — the native snapshot format
docs.text:
An 8-byte header (the magic RSHOT, a format version byte, a compression flag, and a reserved byte), followed by one rkyv-archived payload holding the metadata, the snapshot's own name/path tables, its keys and values, and the deduplicated value data. regshot writes the payload as a single zstd frame. Reading validates the archive before using it, since a .rshot file is untrusted input. After zstd decompression, loading is rkyv's archived access followed by re-interning each name and path into the session, so the same path loaded from two files shares one identity. Splitting the payload into separately compressed sections is a possible future layout change, which would get a new version byte.

Version Contents 1 Metadata, names, paths, keys, values, and value data 2 Version 1's payload unchanged, plus the recorded environment (below) 3 Version 2's payload unchanged, plus the current control set (below) 4 (written today) Version 3's payload unchanged, plus each key's last write time

This build reads all four. Older files just lack what later versions added.

Recorded environment. At capture, regshot shot (and the MCP take_snapshot tool) records the value of each environment variable that the snapshot's REG_EXPAND_SZ values reference with %NAME%. It records only those variables, never the capturing process's whole environment, which routinely holds unrelated credentials. That's enough to show every REG_EXPAND_SZ value expanded later, on any machine, exactly as it would have expanded on the captured one. regshot info lists what a snapshot recorded.

Current control set. HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet is a link to one of the ControlSetNNN keys, the one SYSTEM\Select\Current names. A snapshot holds that control set once, under the name CurrentControlSet, and records which ControlSetNNN it was. Other control sets keep their own names. CurrentControlSet is the name that's correct on every machine, which matters when an undo or installer script is replayed elsewhere. If two compared snapshots recorded different control sets (after a Last Known Good boot, say), regshot diff notes it. regshot info shows the recorded one.

Architecture-independent by construction: a .rshot written by the x86 build is byte-identical to one written by the x64 or ARM64 build from the same input — fixed-width little-endian fields throughout, no usize on the wire — which is what makes it safe to compare snapshots captured on different machines with different builds.

docs.title: Legacy .hiv / .hivu import
docs.text:
Upstream's two incompatible formats (ANSI .hiv, Unicode .hivu) are readable for migration, not writable:

regshot import-hive old.hiv  --out new.rshot   # ANSI,    1.8.x / 1.9.x
regshot import-hive old.hivu --out new.rshot   # Unicode, 1.9.x

Both formats carry a filesystem-entry chain alongside the registry data (addressed by its own offset in the file header, independent of the registry sections), which the importer walks and discards, reporting the count of dropped entries rather than silently losing them — regshot-rs is registry-only. Imported snapshots are tagged with an Unknown WOW64 view, since upstream predates that distinction. Upstream followed the CurrentControlSet link, so its files hold the current control set twice; the import keeps one copy, as described above.

docs.title: .reg (v4 / v5)
docs.text: REGEDIT4 (ANSI) and Windows Registry Editor Version 5.00 (Unicode, UTF-16LE with BOM). See Undo scripts and installers for the WOW64-view caveat that applies to this format specifically.

docs.title: JSON / NDJSON
docs.text:
json emits a structured timeline for tooling. It's the same report model the HTML page embeds.

ndjson-ecs (regshot diff --template ndjson-ecs) emits one Elastic Common Schema 9.5 event per change, one JSON object per line, ready for a SIEM ingest pipeline:

Field Value @timestamp When the "to" snapshot was captured (omitted if it recorded no time) event.kind / event.category / event.type event / ["registry"] / ["creation"], ["deletion"] or ["change"] event.action key-added, key-deleted, value-added, value-deleted, value-modified event.module / event.dataset regshot / regshot.diff registry.hive, .key, .path, .value e.g. HKLM, SOFTWARE\Foo, HKLM\SOFTWARE\Foo\Bar, Bar registry.data.type REG_SZ, REG_DWORD, … registry.data.strings String types decoded (one entry per REG_MULTI_SZ item); DWORD/QWORD as decimal registry.data.bytes Base64, for every other type host.name / user.name From the "to" snapshot, when recorded regshot.category, .view, .interesting, .transition, .previous.data The change category, WOW64 view, known-interesting rule, snapshot pair, and a modification's old value

registry.data is the value after the change, or the last value before a deletion. --generalize and --only-interesting apply as they do to the report. String data is carried only as strings, never also as bytes, because raw bytes would bring back the per-user paths that generalization removes. The MCP generate_report tool accepts ndjson-ecs too.

Every template, built-in or your own, can show text in the report's language. regshot diff uses --lang or the settings file's [ui] language. The MCP server always renders in English.

docs.text: Filter Effect esc_name Escapes a name per the template's [escapes.name] table esc_data Escapes value data per [escapes.data] reg_literal Renders a value as its format-appropriate literal ("…", dword:…, hex bytes)

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
{% for key, changes in timeline.by_key(direction) %}
[{{ key.path }}]
{%- for c in changes %}
{%- if c.kind == "ValDel" %}
"{{ c.name | esc_name }}"=-
{%- else %}
"{{ c.name | esc_name }}"={{ c.value | reg_literal }}
{%- endif %}
{%- endfor %}
{% endfor %}
